procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated the 30th October, 1980 of the High Court of Allahabad in Capital Reference No. 1 of 1980 in Criminal Appeals Nos. 43 & 70 of 1980 & 62 of 1980.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge convicted Dr. V.K. Saxena under sections 120-B, 302 and 201 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to death for murder. Bhagwati Singh was convicted under section 120-B and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court reduced Dr. Saxena's death sentence to life imprisonment because the two judges differed on the question of his guilt. The High Court acquitted Bhagwati Singh.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Dr. Saxena filed Special Leave Petition No. 3372 of 1980 challenging his conviction and sentence. The State of U.P. filed Special Leave Petition No. 581 of 1981 contending that Dr. Saxena should be sentenced to death. The State of U.P. also filed Special Leave Petition No. 582 of 1981 against the High Court's acquittal of Bhagwati Singh. The Supreme Court dismissed all three petitions.

directions: Dismissing the petition of the accused and the States petitions against the acquittal of the co-accused and for. enhancement of the sentence to death sentence.
Special Leave Petition No. 3372 of 1980 must therefore be dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether special leave to appeal can be granted against a conviction when the circumstantial evidence on record proves the motive and connects the accused to the crime and its concealment.

facts: Dr. Saxena was convicted for the murder of his wife, Sudha, based on circumstantial evidence.
The evidence showed a clear motive: Dr. Saxena was having an illicit affair with a nurse and used to harass and assault his wife.

After the murder, Dr. Saxena's conduct included buying a box, packing his wife's dead body into it, attempting to dispose of it in the Ganges river, and then falsely reporting to family and police that she had run away.
law: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has discretionary power to grant a special leave to appeal.
The Court will not grant a special leave to appeal against a conviction if the circumstantial evidence on record is sufficient to prove the case against the accused.
application: The Court found that the evidence of Dr. Saxena's illicit affair and his harassment of his wife constituted the "clearest evidence" of motive.
The Court determined that Dr. Saxena's actions after the death—packing the body in a box, attempting to dispose of it, and filing false reports—clearly connected him to the crime and its concealment.
The Court concluded that this conduct was "tell-tale evidence of the dastardly murder" and refuted any possibility that the wife had committed suicide.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the special leave to appeal because the circumstantial evidence was strong enough to prove the motive for the murder and to connect the accused, Dr. Saxena, to the commission of the crime and his subsequent attempts to conceal it. Therefore, the Court found no reason to interfere with the conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether special leave to appeal can be granted to enhance a sentence from life imprisonment to death, when the High Court reduced the sentence because the two judges differed on the question of the guilt of the accused.

facts: The Sessions Court convicted the accused, Dr. Saxena, of murder and sentenced him to death.
On appeal, the case was heard by a two-judge bench of the High Court.
The two High Court judges differed on the fundamental question of whether Dr. Saxena was guilty.
Because of this disagreement on guilt, the High Court reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment.
The State then petitioned the Supreme Court, asking for special leave to appeal to enhance the sentence back to death.
law: The Supreme Court's power to hear such a petition is governed by Order XXI, Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, and Article 136 of the Constitution.
The High Court's action to reduce the sentence was based on Sections 392 and 370 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Crl. P.C.).
application: The Supreme Court noted that the death sentence imposed by the Sessions Judge may have been justified, and stated that it would not have interfered if the High Court had upheld that sentence.
However, the Court was faced with a specific situation: the High Court had reduced the sentence for the sole reason that the two judges could not agree on the accused's guilt.

The Court reasoned that in such a circumstance, where there is judicial disagreement at the High Court level regarding the guilt of the accused, the Supreme Court cannot interfere to increase the sentence from life imprisonment back to death.
The Court stated it did not "feel called upon to restore the sentence of death" given this specific factual and procedural background.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the State's petition, concluding that it cannot grant special leave to appeal to enhance a sentence from life imprisonment to death when the High Court's reason for reducing the sentence was a difference of opinion between its two judges on the guilt of the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether special leave to appeal can be granted against a conviction when the circumstantial evidence on record proves the motive and connects the accused to the crime and its concealment.
appellant_arguments: The accused (Dr. Saxena) argued that the victim might have committed suicide by hanging, and his actions were merely to destroy the evidence of that suicide, which does not constitute an offence.
respondent_arguments: The State argued that the accused's conduct after the victim's death was inconsistent with the theory of suicide. His actions—buying a box, packing the body, transporting it by train, throwing it into the Ganges, and then filing false reports that his wife had run away—formed a chain of circumstantial evidence proving he committed a dastardly murder.

arguments.issue_text: Whether special leave to appeal can be granted to enhance a sentence from life imprisonment to death, when the High Court reduced the sentence because the two judges differed on the question of the guilt of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The State argued that the accused must be sentenced to death, as the death sentence was justifiably imposed by the Sessions Judge for the heinous crime committed.
respondent_arguments: The accused's position was that the life sentence should be upheld because the High Court reduced the death sentence for the specific reason that the two judges on the bench differed on the fundamental question of his guilt.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Special Leave to appeal cannot be granted against a conviction and sentence when the circumstantial evidence on record proves the motive and connects the accused to the crime and its concealment, and when the High Court has reduced a death sentence to life imprisonment because the two judges differed on the question of the accused's guilt.
obiter: If the High Court were to uphold the sentence of death, the Supreme Court would not have interfered with that sentence.
There is not the slightest doubt that Bhagwati Singh is the root cause of the murder of Sudha, wife of her paramour Dr. Saxena.
Sudha's murder was a consummation which Bhagwati Singh must have devoutly wished for.

We, therefore, dismiss the special leave petition though not without expressing our severe resentment against the overall conduct of Bhagwati Singh. She, like Dr. Saxena, has disgraced a noble profession. Together, they are responsible for the murder of an innocent woman - one morally and the other legally.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the accused's appeal against conviction was dismissed because his conduct after the victim's death—including concealing the body and filing false reports—formed a complete chain of evidence proving his guilt and disproving his suicide theory. The State's appeal to enhance the sentence from life imprisonment to death was also dismissed because the Supreme Court will not interfere with a sentence reduction made by the High Court for the reason that its two judges differed on the fundamental question of the accused's guilt.
legal_tests_applied: Order XXI Rule 6, read with Article 136 of the Constitution - The standard for granting Special Leave to Appeal, which requires the Court to determine if the case warrants interference.

Chain of Circumstantial Evidence - The principle that in a case resting on circumstantial evidence, the evidence must form a complete chain that points exclusively to the guilt of the accused and is inconsistent with any hypothesis of innocence.
why_appellant_lost: The accused's (Dr. Saxena's) appeal against his conviction failed because his theory that the victim committed suicide was contradicted by the evidence. The court found it was 'plain logic' that his subsequent actions—'buying a box packing the dead body of his wife into that box, travelling with that box... throwing the box on way into the Ganges... and finally lodging a false and misleading reports'—were entirely inconsistent with the victim having committed suicide.

The State's appeal to enhance the sentence to death failed because the Supreme Court refused to interfere in a situation where the High Court reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment for the specific reason that 'the two learned Judges differed on the question as to the guilt of the accused.' The court stated that in such circumstances, it 'cannot interf~~re under Order XXI against the sentence.'
why_respondent_won: The State (as respondent in the conviction appeal) won because the court accepted its argument that the circumstantial evidence proved the accused's guilt. The court found a clear motive in the accused's 'illicit affair with the co-accused' and concluded that his conduct after the death 'contained tell-tale evidence of the dastardly murder of a defenceless woman.'

The accused (as respondent in the sentence enhancement appeal) won because the court upheld the High Court's decision to impose life imprisonment instead of death. The court accepted the premise that the lack of unanimity between the High Court judges on the core issue of guilt was a sufficient reason to reduce the sentence, and it would not 'feel called upon to restore the sentence of death' in that context.
policy_considerations: The court exercises judicial restraint in capital punishment cases, refusing to enhance a sentence to death when there was a difference of opinion on the fundamental question of guilt among the judges of the High Court. The court stated, 'Faced with such a situation where the death sentence... is reduced to life imprison1nent by the Hiah Court... for the reason that the two learned Judges differed on the question as to the auilt of the accused, the Supreme Court cannot interf~~re against the sentence.'
